items.title: Home
items.text:
Python · Jinja · static output

Version 2.0

This documentation covers the 2.0 engine. Projects built with 1.x need the conversion described in Migration from 1.x.

items.title: Write Markdown. Ship a site.
items.text:
jamstack turns a folder of Markdown and Jinja templates into a fast static site. Three runtime dependencies, no JavaScript toolchain, and no network access during a build.

Start the tutorial Install

items.title: Install
items.text:
python -m pip install jamstack

Python 3.11 or newer.

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
jamstack init my-site --theme blog
cd my-site
jamstack build
jamstack serve

Your site lands in dist/ and is served at http://127.0.0.1:8000/. Edit anything under content/ and the page rebuilds on the next save.

items.title: What you get
items.text:
Markdown or Jinja. Posts in Markdown with TOML front matter, or an .html file when you want full control of the markup.

Themes as folders. Two ship with the package. Override one in your project or write your own.

A real dev loop. Rebuilds on change, debounces rapid saves, and keeps the last good build when a template fails.

The boring essentials. sitemap.xml, an Atom feed, clean URLs and a themed 404.html, generated from the same sources.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• Tutorial — build a blog from an empty folder in a few minutes.
  • Content — front matter, URL rules, drafts and HTML pages.
  • Configuration — every key in site.toml.
  • Themes — the theme format and the template API.
  • Command line — commands, options and exit codes.
  • Deployment — GitHub Pages, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages.
  • Migration from 1.x — convert a settings.py/static.py project.
  • Contributing — local setup and project conventions.

items.title: Command line
items.text:
jamstack [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]

Run jamstack --help or jamstack <command> --help for the same reference in the terminal. python -m jamstack behaves identically.

items.title: jamstack init
items.text:
Create a new site.

jamstack init [PATH] [--theme NAME] [--force]
Option Default Meaning PATH . Directory to create the site in. --theme NAME minimal Theme to scaffold with. Use jamstack themes to list them. --force off Write into a non-empty directory.

It creates site.toml, content/index.md, and a .gitignore with dist/ plus any files the theme ships in its scaffold/ directory. It refuses to write into a file, or into a non-empty directory without --force.

jamstack init my-blog --theme blog

items.title: jamstack build
items.text:
Build the site into the configured output directory.

jamstack build [--clean] [--drafts]
Option Meaning --clean Delete the output directory before building. --drafts Include pages with draft = true.

Reports how many pages were built. Use --clean when you have deleted or renamed pages and want their old output gone.

items.title: jamstack serve
items.text:
Build, serve the output, and rebuild when sources change.

jamstack serve [--port PORT] [--drafts]
Option Default Meaning --port PORT 8000 Port to bind on 127.0.0.1. 0 picks any free port. --drafts off Include drafts.

The server watches site.toml, content/, templates/, static/, and the active theme's directories. Changes are debounced: a burst of saves produces one rebuild. If a rebuild fails, the error is printed and the previous build keeps being served.

Stop it with Ctrl+C.

items.title: jamstack themes
items.text:
List the themes available to the current project, marking each as bundled or local, with the description from its manifest.

jamstack themes

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
Code Meaning 0 Success. 1 A user-facing error: missing site.toml, invalid content, template failure, port in use. 2 Invalid usage: unknown command or option.

Errors go to standard error, so jamstack build can be used in scripts and CI without parsing output.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
site.toml lives at the project root and is the only configuration file. It must exist before jamstack build; jamstack init creates it.

[site]
title = "My Site"
description = "Notes on small tools."
author = "Your Name"
base_url = "https://example.com"
language = "en"

[build]
output = "dist"

[theme]
name = "blog"

items.title: [site]
items.text:
Key Required Default Used for title yes — Site name in templates, feed title, generated site.toml. description no "" Meta description in themes, feed subtitle. author no "" Feed author. Falls back to title when empty. base_url no "" Absolute URL for sitemap.xml and feed.xml. language no "en" lang attribute in themes.

title is trimmed and cannot be empty; the build stops with [site].title is required if it is.

items.title: base_url
items.text:
Set it to the public URL of the deployed site, including the scheme and without a trailing slash:

base_url = "https://example.com"

When it is set, the build writes sitemap.xml with every page and feed.xml with every dated page. When it is empty, both files are skipped: emitting a sitemap with relative URLs is invalid, and silently inventing a domain is worse.

If the site is published under a subpath, include it: https://example.com/blog.

items.title: [build]
items.text:
Key Default Meaning output "dist" Directory where the generated site is written, relative to the project root.

The output directory is replaced file by file on each build. Use jamstack build --clean to delete it first, which removes files left over from pages you deleted.

items.title: [theme]
items.text:
Key Default Meaning name "minimal" Theme to render with.

The name must match ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*$. Jamstack resolves it from <project>/themes/<name>/ first and falls back to the themes bundled with the package. See Themes.

items.title: [extra]
items.text:
Free-form table for values your theme needs. Jamstack does not interpret it: templates read it as site.extra.

[extra]
footer_text = "Built with jamstack"

[extra.social]
github = "https://github.com/jamstackpy"

It must be a table; any other type stops the build with an error. Themes render with StrictUndefined, so read optional keys with site.extra.get("...") instead of site.extra.key.

items.title: Behaviour worth knowing
items.text:
• Unknown keys are ignored, so a future version can add options without breaking old files.
  • Relative paths are resolved from the project root, not from the current directory; commands must be run inside the project.
  • jamstack serve watches site.toml, so editing it triggers a rebuild like any content change.
  • The file is parsed with tomllib; invalid TOML stops the build and reports the file and line.

items.title: Content
items.text: Everything under content/ becomes the site. The engine reads .md and .html files recursively; any other file is ignored.

items.title: Files and URLs
items.text:
The path of a file determines its URL and its output file:

Source URL Output content/index.md / dist/index.html content/about.md /about/ dist/about/index.html content/posts/hello.md /posts/hello/ dist/posts/hello/index.html content/posts/2026/index.md /posts/2026/ dist/posts/2026/index.html

A file named index maps to its directory instead of a subdirectory, which is what makes clean URLs work. Two sources that resolve to the same output fail the build instead of overwriting each other silently.

items.title: Front matter
items.text:
Markdown and HTML pages can start with TOML front matter between +++ lines:

+++
title = "Why static sites"
date = 2026-11-07
summary = "No runtime, no database, no surprises."
template = "post"
+++

The body starts here.

Front matter is optional. Without it, the title is derived from the file name (second-post.md becomes "Second Post") and the default template is used.

items.title: Recognised keys
items.text:
Key Type Default Meaning title string File name Page title. date ISO date none Publication date. Drives ordering and feeds. template string index or page Template file, with or without .html. draft boolean false Skipped unless the build uses --drafts. summary string none Short description used by the blog theme and the feed. url string Derived from the file Public URL, starting with / and ending in / or .html.

Any other key is kept in page.meta and is available to templates, so a theme can support cover, tags, or anything else without engine changes.

items.title: URLs
items.text:
By default the URL comes from the file path: about.md becomes /about/ and posts/hello.md becomes /posts/hello/. Use url in the front matter to publish a page somewhere else:

+++
title = "Changelog"
url = "/changelog/"
+++

The value must start with / and end in / or .html; anything else fails the build instead of being silently ignored.

File names are used as written, including non-ASCII characters: año-nuevo.md is published at /año-nuevo/. Keep that in mind when choosing names, because changing one changes the URL.

items.title: Dates
items.text: date accepts a TOML date (2026-11-07), a TOML datetime, or an ISO string. Only the calendar date is used; times are discarded. An invalid value fails the build with the source file in the message.

items.title: Drafts
items.text:
A page with draft = true is loaded but excluded from the build. To preview it locally:

jamstack build --drafts
jamstack serve --drafts

Be careful not to deploy a dist/ built with --drafts: drafts are included in the sitemap and the feed.

items.title: Markdown
items.text:
Markdown is parsed as CommonMark with raw HTML enabled, so inline HTML works:

A paragraph with a <mark>highlight</mark>.

<div class="note">A block written in HTML.</div>

The rendered HTML is exposed to templates as page.content, already marked safe. Do not add |safe to it.

items.title: HTML pages
items.text:
A .html file is rendered as a Jinja template instead of Markdown. It receives the same variables as any other page (site, page, pages), which makes it useful for landing pages with custom markup:

+++
title = "Landing"
+++

<section class="hero">
  <h1>{{ site.title }}</h1>
  <p>{{ site.description }}</p>
</section>

<ul>
  {% for item in pages if item.url != "/" %}
    <li><a href="{{ item.url }}">{{ item.title }}</a></li>
  {% endfor %}
</ul>

items.title: Page order
items.text: Templates receive pages sorted by date, newest first, then by title. Pages without a date sort after dated pages. The blog theme filters that list to dated pages, which is why an about page does not appear among the posts.

items.title: Errors you will see
items.text:
• invalid front matter: the TOML between +++ lines does not parse.
  • unterminated front matter: the opening +++ has no closing line.
  • invalid date: the value is not an ISO date.
  • both build to …: two files resolve to the same output path.

All of them stop the build and name the source file. The development server keeps serving the last successful build while you fix the file.

items.title: Contributing
items.text: The project is developed on the stable branch. Bug reports and pull requests go to github.com/jamstackpy/jamstack.

items.title: Local setup
items.text:
git clone git@github.com:jamstackpy/jamstack.git
cd jamstack
git switch stable
python -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit --hook-type commit-msg

items.title: Checks
items.text:
ruff check .
ruff format --check .
pytest

The same checks run in CI on Python 3.11 through 3.14. A pull request that changes behaviour needs a test that would fail without the change.

items.title: Commits
items.text:
Commits follow Conventional Commits in English:

feat(cli): add a --drafts flag to build
fix(content): reject dates without a year
docs: explain local theme overrides

One commit is one reviewable intention. Put mechanical changes (renames, formatting, dependency bumps) in their own commit, and do not leave intermediate commits that fail the tests. When the change needs context, add a bullet-point body explaining what and why.

commitizen validates the message through the commit-msg hook.

items.title: Pull requests
items.text:
• Target stable.
  • Keep user-facing text and documentation in English.
  • Do not rewrite pushed history.

The full guide, including the release process, lives in CONTRIBUTING.md.

items.title: Deployment
items.text:
A build produces a folder of static files. There is nothing to run on the server: upload dist/ to any host that serves files, and that is the whole deployment.

Three things to check before the final build:

  1. base_url in site.toml is the real public URL.
  2. The final build uses --clean, so deleted pages do not linger.
  3. dist/ is not committed (the generated .gitignore already excludes it).
jamstack build --clean

items.title: GitHub Pages
items.text:
The most direct setup is a workflow that builds on every push and publishes with the official Pages actions. In the site repository, create .github/workflows/pages.yml:

name: Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.13"
      - run: pip install jamstack
      - run: jamstack build --clean
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: dist
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

Then set the repository's Pages source to GitHub Actions.

For a project site served under https://user.github.io/repo/, set base_url to that full URL including the subpath, so the sitemap and feed links resolve correctly.

If you publish by pushing a gh-pages branch instead, add an empty .nojekyll file to dist/ so GitHub Pages does not preprocess the output.

items.title: Netlify
items.text:
Setting Value Build command pip install jamstack && jamstack build --clean Publish directory dist

Netlify's build image must provide Python 3.11 or newer. If it does not, build the site in your own CI and deploy the resulting dist/ as a prebuilt site.

items.title: Cloudflare Pages
items.text:
Setting Value Framework preset None Build command pip install jamstack && jamstack build --clean Build output directory dist

As with Netlify, if the build image lacks a suitable Python, build elsewhere and upload dist/ directly.

items.title: Any other host
items.text:
Copy the contents of dist/ to the web root. Two details depend on the host:

  • Clean URLs. The site writes about/index.html, which every common host serves at /about/. A host that only maps /about/ to /about.html needs a rewrite rule, but this is rare.
  • 404 pages. dist/404.html is produced when the active theme provides a 404.html template. GitHub Pages, Netlify, and Cloudflare Pages pick it up automatically; other hosts may need to be told the filename.

items.title: Caching
items.text: Every build writes the same paths with new contents. If your host caches aggressively, either purge the cache on deploy or give the HTML a short Cache-Control and the assets a long one. Asset filenames are not hashed yet, so immutable caching on /style.css will keep serving stale CSS after a deploy.

items.title: Migrating from 1.x to 2.0
items.text:
2.0 is a rewrite of the engine, not an update. The 1.x model — a copy of static.py and settings.py inside every project, themes downloaded from GitHub, Flask declared as a dependency — is gone. Projects built with 1.x do not run on 2.0 without conversion, and there is no automated converter.

This guide walks through the conversion. Keep the 1.x site running with python -m pip install "jamstack<2" until the new build looks right.

items.title: What changed
items.text:
1.x 2.0 jamstack plain <name> jamstack init <name> jamstack t html5up/massively <name> jamstack init <name> --theme blog (or your own theme) settings.py with OUTPUT_FOLDER site.toml with [build] output posts.json one Markdown file per post with front matter python static.py jamstack build python static.py --serve jamstack serve --watch and --port flags watch is automatic; --port still exists --jamdo asset downloader removed; themes ship their own assets html5up themes removed from the package Jinja context with info and posts site, page, pages Python 3.6+ Python 3.11+

Flask is no longer a dependency. It was declared in 1.x but never imported by the code.

items.title: Step 1: create a 2.0 project
items.text:
Do not convert in place. Create a parallel project and copy into it:

jamstack init new-site --theme minimal

Use --theme blog if the site is a dated blog. Both themes are documented in themes.md.

items.title: Step 2: convert settings.py
items.text:
1.x projects carry a settings.py that points at the output directory and sometimes at JSON data. Everything configurable now lives in site.toml:

[site]
title = "My Site"
description = "What the site is about"
base_url = "https://example.com"

[build]
output = "dist"

[theme]
name = "minimal"

Set base_url only when you know the public URL; it enables sitemap.xml and feed.xml.

items.title: Step 3: convert posts.json
items.text:
In 1.x every post was an entry in posts.json that pointed at a template file. In 2.0 each post is a file under content/:

+++
title = "My first post"
date = 2026-11-06
summary = "A short description for listings and feeds."
+++

The body, in Markdown.

The path determines the URL: content/posts/my-first-post.md becomes /posts/my-first-post/. Drafts get draft = true and are skipped unless you build with --drafts.

items.title: Step 4: bring your templates
items.text:
If you used a bundled html5up theme, it no longer exists in 2.0. You have two options:

  1. Redesign with the minimal or blog theme and move content into their structure.
  2. Keep your 1.x templates by turning them into a local theme:
new-site/
  themes/
    legacy/
      theme.toml
      templates/
        index.html
        page.html
        ...
      static/
        assets/

theme.toml:

name = "legacy"
description = "Templates imported from my 1.x site."

Then set [theme] name = "legacy" in site.toml. Templates that extended base.html keep working as long as you adjust the variables:

  • page.title, page.content, page.date, page.meta for the current page.
  • pages for every page in the build, already sorted.
  • site.title, site.description, site.language for global values.

The Jinja environment is now strict: a missing variable fails the build instead of rendering an empty string. That is intentional — it catches typos that 1.x silently ignored.

items.title: Step 5: move assets to static/
items.text: Anything the templates load by path — CSS, images, fonts — belongs in static/. Its contents are copied to the root of dist/, so static/assets/site.css is served at /assets/site.css. Project files overwrite the theme's files with the same path.

items.title: Step 6: build and compare
items.text:
jamstack build
jamstack serve --port 8000

Check the URL map: 1.x wrote one HTML file per source template, while 2.0 turns content/about.md into dist/about/index.html (clean URLs by default). If your host expects .html paths, adjust the template links, not the engine.

items.title: If you keep html5up templates
items.text: The html5up designs that shipped with 1.x are licensed CC BY 3.0, which requires visible attribution. They are not part of the 2.0 package. If you import them as a local theme, keep the original credits in the footer.

items.title: Getting help
items.text: Open an issue with the 1.x site.toml equivalent, the template that fails, and the full error output. The stable branch still contains the 1.x source for reference.

items.title: Theme specification
items.text:
A theme is a directory. Jamstack resolves it from the project first and falls back to the themes bundled with the package:

<project>/themes/<name>/     # wins if present
src/jamstack/themes/<name>/  # bundled with the package

<name> must match the name field in the manifest and the [theme] name value in site.toml.

items.title: Directory layout
items.text:
mytheme/
  theme.toml        # required
  templates/        # required
  static/           # optional
  scaffold/         # optional

items.title: theme.toml
items.text:
name = "mytheme"
description = "A one-line description shown by 'jamstack themes'."

Both fields are strings. name is required and must equal the directory name; description is optional.

items.title: templates/
items.text:
Jinja templates rendered with autoescaping enabled for .html and .xml and with StrictUndefined, so referencing a missing variable fails the build instead of rendering an empty string.

The engine picks the template for each page in this order:

  1. The template key from the page's front matter.
  2. index.html if the page is an index file, otherwise page.html.

The template value may omit the .html extension.

Templates receive three variables:

Variable Type Contents site config object title, description, author, base_url, language, output, theme, root page page object title, url, date, draft, meta, content, source, output, template pages list of pages Every page in the build, sorted by date descending, then title ascending

page.content is already rendered and marked safe: Markdown for .md files, Jinja output for .html files. Wrap it in {{ page.content }} without a |safe filter.

page.meta holds every front matter key, so themes can define their own conventions (summary, cover, tags, …) without engine changes.

items.title: static/
items.text: Copied recursively into the output root after the pages are written. If the project also has a static/ directory, the project's files are copied second and overwrite the theme's, which is the supported way to replace a logo or a stylesheet without forking the theme.

items.title: scaffold/
items.text: Copied into the project only during jamstack init, before the generated site.toml and starter content are written. Use it to ship example posts, images, or a content/ structure that makes sense for the theme. It is never read during a build.

items.title: 404.html (optional)
items.text: If the theme provides templates/404.html, the engine renders it to dist/404.html using site and pages. Static hosts such as GitHub Pages, Netlify, and Cloudflare Pages serve that file automatically.

items.title: Template overrides
items.text: The project's own templates/ directory is searched before the theme's. To tweak one file without copying the whole theme, create <project>/templates/page.html; the rest keeps coming from the theme.

items.title: Starting from a bundled theme
items.text:
To change a bundled theme's structure, copy it into the project and edit the copy. Local themes win over bundled ones with the same name:

mkdir -p themes
cp -r "$(python -c 'import jamstack, pathlib; print(pathlib.Path(jamstack.__file__).parent / "themes" / "blog")')" themes/blog

The project now has themes/blog/ with the same name, so [theme] name = "blog" keeps working and the local files take over.

items.title: Minimal theme
items.text:
mytheme/
  theme.toml
  templates/
    base.html
    index.html
    page.html
  static/
    style.css

theme.toml

name = "mytheme"
description = "The smallest possible theme."

templates/base.html

<!doctype html>
<html lang="{{ site.language }}">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>{% block title %}{{ site.title }}{% endblock %}</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">
  </head>
  <body>
    {% block content %}{% endblock %}
  </body>
</html>

templates/page.html

{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}{{ page.title }} · {{ site.title }}{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  <article>
    <h1>{{ page.title }}</h1>
    {{ page.content }}
  </article>
{% endblock %}

templates/index.html

{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>{{ page.title }}</h1>
  {{ page.content }}
  <ul>
    {% for item in pages if item.url != "/" %}
      <li><a href="{{ item.url }}">{{ item.title }}</a></li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
{% endblock %}

Set [theme] name = "mytheme" in site.toml and run jamstack build.

items.title: Rules the engine enforces
items.text:
• A theme without theme.toml or templates/ is rejected.
  • The manifest name must match the directory name.
  • A missing template, or an undefined variable in a template, fails the build with the offending file and line.
  • A page whose output path collides with another page fails the build.

items.title: Tutorial: build a blog
items.text: This walks through a complete site: scaffold it, write two posts, add an about page, change the look, and generate the feed. Every command is safe to run in an empty directory.

items.title: 1. Create the site
items.text:
jamstack init my-blog --theme blog
cd my-blog

Created site in my-blog using the 'blog' theme
Next steps:
  cd my-blog
  jamstack build

You get a small tree:

my-blog/
  site.toml
  content/
    index.md
    posts/hello-world.md
  .gitignore

site.toml is the only configuration file. content/ holds the pages. The theme lives inside the package, so your project stays clean.

items.title: 2. Build it
items.text:
jamstack build

Built 2 page(s) into /home/you/my-blog/dist

Two pages: the home page and the example post. Now serve it:

jamstack serve

Built 2 page(s) into /home/you/my-blog/dist
Serving at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ (Ctrl+C to stop)

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/. Leave it running: every time you save a file under content/, templates/, static/, or site.toml, the site rebuilds. If a template breaks, the terminal reports the error and the browser keeps showing the last working build.

items.title: 3. Write a post
items.text:
Create content/posts/second-post.md:

+++
title = "Why static sites"
date = 2026-11-07
summary = "No runtime, no database, no surprises."
template = "post"
+++

A static site is a folder of files. That is the whole trick.

- Nothing to patch at 3 a.m.
- Nothing to scale.
- Nothing to leak.

Save it and reload. The home page lists the post with its date and summary, and the post is available at /posts/second-post/.

The front matter is TOML between +++ lines. title and date are the ones that matter here: the blog theme lists only dated pages, newest first, and the feed only includes them.

items.title: 4. Add an about page
items.text:
Create content/about.md:

+++
title = "About"
template = "page"
+++

I write about small tools and static sites.

It is published at /about/. Because it has no date, it does not appear in the post list. Link it from the home page by editing content/index.md:

+++
title = "Welcome"
+++

Notes on small tools.

[About this site](/about/)

items.title: 5. Describe the site
items.text:
Open site.toml and fill it in:

[site]
title = "Small Tools"
description = "Notes on small tools and static sites."
author = "Your Name"
base_url = "https://example.com"
language = "en"

[build]
output = "dist"

[theme]
name = "blog"

base_url is the public URL of the site. Set it to the real domain when you deploy: it makes the links in sitemap.xml and feed.xml absolute. While it is empty, both files are skipped instead of being written with relative URLs.

After saving, check dist/sitemap.xml, dist/feed.xml, and dist/404.html.

items.title: 6. Change the look
items.text:
For small changes, customize the theme's stylesheet. Files in the project's static/ are copied after the theme's and overwrite the same path, so the theme's /style.css is the file to replace:

jamstack build
mkdir -p static
cp dist/style.css static/style.css

Now edit static/style.css and change the accent color:

:root {
  --accent: #b45309;
}

Run jamstack build again and the site uses your copy. The rest of the theme is untouched.

For structural changes, create a local copy of the theme:

mkdir -p themes
cp -r "$(python -c 'import jamstack, pathlib; print(pathlib.Path(jamstack.__file__).parent / "themes" / "blog")')" themes/blog

Edit themes/blog/templates/ freely. Local themes take precedence over bundled ones with the same name, so no configuration change is needed. See Themes for the template variables and the full format.

items.title: 7. Publish
items.text:
jamstack build --clean

Upload the contents of dist/ to any static host. Deployment has the settings for GitHub Pages, Netlify, and Cloudflare Pages.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Content explains URL mapping, drafts, and HTML pages.
  • Configuration lists every key in site.toml.
  • Command line covers the flags used above.

items.title: Versioning policy
items.text: jamstack follows Semantic Versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.

items.title: What counts as a breaking change
items.text:
A major release is required when an existing site or theme stops working:

  • Renaming or removing a CLI command, option or exit code.
  • Removing or renaming a key in site.toml.
  • Changing the front matter keys, or the URLs that build generates for pages.
  • Changing the template context (site, page, pages) or the required fields of theme.toml.
  • Raising the minimum Python version.

New commands, optional site.toml keys, new template variables and new bundled themes ship in a minor release. Bug fixes ship in a patch release; a patch never changes behaviour on purpose.

items.title: Deprecations
items.text:
A feature is deprecated before it is removed:

  1. The changelog and the reference page mark it deprecated.
  2. It keeps working for at least one minor release.
  3. It is removed in the next major release.

When the engine can detect the old usage, the CLI prints a deprecation warning instead of failing silently.

items.title: Supported versions
items.text:
Only the latest major release receives fixes. 2.x is the current line; 1.x is unsupported. If a 3.0 is released, 2.x will receive security fixes for six months after that release.

Python 3.11 or newer is required. Support for a Python version is dropped in a minor release once that version reaches end of life.

items.title: Documentation versions
items.text:
This site documents the latest release. The documentation for a specific version is available from its tag:

https://github.com/jamstackpy/jamstack/tree/v2.0.0/docs
